name: Gernika Peace Museum (Museo de la Paz)
text: On the afternoon of Monday 26 April 1937 – market day – aircraft of the German Condor Legion, with Italian Aviazione Legionaria bombers, attacked Gernika for about three hours in support of the Nationalist advance on Bilbao. Explosive and incendiary bombs destroyed most of the town centre, while the Rentería bridge and the arms factories on the edge of town survived. The raid, reported worldwide by journalists including George Steer and painted by Picasso, became the defining image of the bombing of civilians. The Peace Museum, on the main square, tells the story of the raid through survivors' testimony and places it in a wider history of war and reconciliation, including Germany's 1997 apology.
look: A modern museum with a reconstructed 1937 house interior, survivor testimony, audiovisuals and a section on peace and reconciliation.
plan: Foru Plaza 1, opposite the town hall. Closed Mondays; small entry fee (about €5); English group tours can be booked in advance.
disputed: Death toll: the Basque Government reported 1,645 dead in 1937; most modern historians put it between about 126 and 300; Xabier Irujo (2017) argues for a much higher figure. Records were destroyed and both sides used the numbers for propaganda.

name: Casa de Juntas & Tree of Gernika
text: The Assembly House (Casa de Juntas) and the oak of Gernika are the historic symbols of Biscayan and Basque self-government: the Lords of Biscay swore under the tree to respect local liberties. That symbolism is one reason the destruction of the town in April 1937 caused such outrage. The assembly house and the oak, then the tree planted in 1860, survived the bombing on the hill above the burning centre. After the Nationalists took the town on 29 April, Carlist requetés of the Tercio de Begoña, themselves Biscayans, posted a guard to stop the tree being damaged. The old trunk stands under a colonnade next to its successor.
look: The 19th-century Assembly House with its stained-glass ceiling, the living oak (planted 2015), and the preserved trunk of the 'old tree' that survived 1937.
plan: Free entry; the Assembly House is usually open daily except some holidays. It's a 5-minute uphill walk from the Peace Museum.

name: Artxanda – Iron Belt trenches & memorial
text: Mount Artxanda, above Bilbao, was the last defended position before the city fell. After the Nationalists broke through the Iron Belt (Cinturón de Hierro) at Gaztelumendi on 12 June 1937, Basque and Republican units fell back to Artxanda, where there was a final, bitter defence while civilians were evacuated westwards. The Basque Army withdrew on 18 June and Nationalist troops entered Bilbao on 19 June. Today the summit is a park with a viewpoint over the city. A stretch of restored trench recalls the fighting, and a large 'fingerprint' sculpture (Huella Dactilar) by Juan José Novella honours all those who died in the war.
look: A restored trench section near the Artxanda viewpoint, the fingerprint memorial and a panoramic view over Bilbao.
plan: Take the Artxanda funicular from central Bilbao (about 3 min) or drive up; free, open access. Allow an hour to walk between the viewpoint and the memorial.

name: Durango bombing – Santa María de Uribarri
text: On 31 March 1937, the first day of General Mola's offensive against Biscay, Italian Savoia-Marchetti S.81 bombers with German and Italian escorts attacked Durango, a road and rail junction behind the front. The first wave struck at about 8 a.m., during morning Mass. The Jesuit church and the Santa Susana convent were hit and priests, nuns and worshippers were killed; Santa María de Uribarri was also damaged. Further raids followed that day. Durango was bombed almost four weeks before Gernika and is often called its forgotten precursor. The town's bombing route links the damaged churches and memorial plaques.
look: The Uribarri basilica with its large wooden porch, plus plaques and panels on the town's bombing route (Bonbardaketaren ibilbidea) marking the sites hit.
plan: Pick up the bombing-route leaflet at the Durango tourist office; the centre is compact and easy to walk in about an hour.
disputed: Deaths are given as about 250 in most accounts; Spanish-language studies give a range of 248–336.

name: Intxorta front & Elgeta memory centre
text: After the loss of most of Gipuzkoa in 1936, Basque and Republican battalions stabilised the front on the Intxorta heights above Elgeta. They held these trenches through the winter and resisted the first weeks of Mola's spring 1937 offensive, until the line had to be abandoned in late April 1937 as the front collapsed towards Durango and Bilbao. Intxorta became a symbol of Basque resistance. The Basque Centre for the Interpretation of Historical Memory in Elgeta explains the fighting and the recovery of memory, and a signposted route leads to restored trenches, shelters and the 'Intxortako Atea' monument.
look: An interpretation centre in the village and a 5.8 km waymarked loop with restored trenches, shelters, viewpoints, the Intxortako Atea monument and the Salvador hermitage.
plan: Guided walks (about 3.5 h) usually run on the first and last Sunday of the month from the Espaloia café-theatre at 10:00; book on 943 71 89 11. The 'Elgeta memoria' app supports self-guided visits.
disputed: The exact date of the final withdrawal from Intxorta is given differently (roughly 20–24 April 1937); check against local sources.

name: Santander air-raid shelter (Refugio Antiaéreo)
text: Santander, then in the Republican zone, was bombed repeatedly during 1937, and over a hundred shelters were dug beneath the city. This one, under the Plaza del Príncipe (then Plaza de Mariana Pineda), was built in spring 1937. It has three connected galleries for about 70 people, mainly military commanders and city officials. It was abandoned after the war and buried during the rebuilding that followed the great fire of 1941. It was rediscovered in 2006 during works on the Plaza Porticada and opened as a museum in 2014. The city fell to Nationalist and Italian troops on 26 August 1937.
look: About 100 m of restored underground galleries with audiovisuals, period photographs and objects, a Condor Legion airman's equipment and a 250 kg bomb.
plan: Guided visits only, in small groups (about €3). Closed Mondays; book ahead by phone (942 203 099).
disputed: The tourist office says Santander suffered 34 air raids; other counts differ.

name: El Mazuco & Sierra del Cuera
text: After Santander fell, the Nationalists pushed west into Asturias. At the El Mazuco pass and on the limestone heights of the Sierra del Cuera, about 5,000 Republican troops of the XIV Army Corps, many of them CNT militia, held off Navarrese brigades under José Solchaga. Those brigades were far stronger, at about 33,000 men, and were supported by the Condor Legion, Italian units and naval gunfire. The Condor Legion used some of its first carpet-bombing tactics here, but the rugged terrain blunted their effect. Peña Turbina, the highest point of the range, was the last main Republican position; it fell on 22 September, opening eastern Asturias.
look: A small mountain village below rocky heights. Hiking routes such as Alto de la Tornería–Los Resquilones cross the former front line, where informal traces of positions remain.
plan: About 16 km south of Llanes on the AS-115. Stout boots are needed for the karst hillsides; the bar in El Mazucu is the only service.
disputed: Sources give different lengths for the battle, from about 17 days (5/6–22 Sep) to '33 days of combat'.

name: Pasealekua air-raid shelter, Gernika
text: In 1936 Gernika dug four tunnel shelters into the hillside by the market area to protect townspeople from air raids. They were in use on 26 April 1937, when crowds from the Monday market and refugees sheltered here as the bombs fell. Two of the four shelters survive. One unfinished tunnel holds a scale model of the shelter as built; the other has a sound-and-light presentation recreating the experience of the people inside during the raid. It is a short, powerful complement to the Peace Museum.
look: Two restored tunnel shelters about 10 m into the hillside, with a model and an immersive audiovisual.
plan: Entrance on Juan Calzada Kalea, near the Pasealeku park. Visits are through the Gernika tourist office; check times at turismo.gernika-lumo.eus.

name: Gaztelumendi breach – Larrabetzu Iron Belt bunker
text: The Iron Belt was built from late 1936 as a ring of trenches, bunkers and gun positions around Bilbao. It was planned for about 70,000 defenders but held by roughly 30,000, and the engineer Alejandro Goicoechea defected to the Nationalists with its plans, revealing its weak points. On 12 June 1937 the Nationalists concentrated heavy artillery and more than a hundred aircraft on the weak Gaztelumendi sector at Larrabetzu and broke through. A last Basque counter-attack at Mantuliz (Derio) failed, and Bilbao fell a week later. Near Sarrikola a concrete bunker was built into a farmhouse; ongoing excavations here have uncovered more remains of the line.
look: A Civil War bunker built inside a building in the Sarrikola area, near the Gaztelumendi breach sector.
plan: In the rural Sarrikola neighbourhood of Larrabetzu. Treat it as private property and look from the lane; combine it with the Zamudio Iron Belt trail on the same ridge.

name: Iron Belt trail, Zamudio (Berreaga–Gaztelumendi ridge)
text: Zamudio lies directly below the stretch of the Iron Belt where the Nationalists broke through. The fighting of 11–13 June 1937 spread along the Berreaga–Urrusti–Gaztelumendi ridge, and on 12 June the attackers crossed the line and came down into Zamudio. A signposted 11.1 km memory trail, marked with support from Gogora (the Basque Institute for Memory, Coexistence and Human Rights), climbs to the ridge past surviving trenches and machine-gun nests. It is one of the best places to understand what the Iron Belt actually looked like on the ground, and why it failed against massed artillery and aircraft.
look: Original trenches and concrete machine-gun posts along the ridge, with explanatory panels and waymarks.
plan: Start from the panel at the Arroeta car park in Zamudio. The 11 km loop takes about 4 h and is hilly; wear walking boots.

name: Otxandio – Andikona bombing memorial
text: On 22 July 1936, four days after the coup, two Breguet XIX light bombers flown from Recajo (La Rioja) by Ángel Salas Larrazábal and José Muñoz Jiménez bombed and machine-gunned the Andikona square in Otxandio. The square was crowded for the Santa Marina fiestas. About 61 people were killed, most of them civilians and many of them children. Otxandio sat on the front between Biscay and Álava. The raid is often called 'the first Gernika', because it was one of the first air attacks of the war to kill a crowd of civilians. A sculpture in the square honours the victims.
look: The village square (Andikona) with a memorial sculpture to the victims of the bombing.
plan: A small village on the BI-623 between Durango and Vitoria; the square is in the centre, so parking and a 20-minute visit are easy.
disputed: Deaths are recorded as 57–61; Paul Preston cites 84. There is debate over whether this or the 18 July raid on Tetuán was the war's first bombing.

name: San Marcial & the Battle of Irun
text: Mola's Navarrese columns under Colonel Alfonso Beorlegui attacked Irun to cut the Republican north off from France. Their attack was supported by German and Italian aircraft and a few light tanks. Basque militia, CNT units, Asturian miners and some French communist volunteers held the Puntza ridge and the San Marcial hill with its hermitage. France had closed the border, and the defenders ran short of ammunition. San Marcial fell after heavy fighting, and Irun was abandoned on 5 September. Retreating anarchists set parts of the town on fire. Beorlegui was wounded entering the town and later died. The Nationalist victory cut Gipuzkoa, Biscay, Santander and Asturias off from the French border.
look: The San Marcial hermitage on its hilltop, with views over Irun, Hendaye and the Bidasoa. Fighting positions are not signposted.
plan: A minor road and footpaths lead up from Irun to the hermitage (about 1 h on foot). The view is best on a clear day.
disputed: The coordinates are for the San Marcial heights (from the 1813 battle article); exact 1936 positions are not marked.

name: Puerto del Escudo – Italian memorial
text: The Escudo pass (about 1,000 m) carries the main road from Burgos to Santander over the Cantabrian range. When the Nationalist offensive on Santander opened on 14 August 1937, Italian CTV divisions attacked here. By 17 August they had taken the pass and linked up with other columns near San Miguel de Aguayo, encircling Republican units. The Santander front collapsed within days, and Santander fell on 26 August. Basque units surrendered to the Italians under the separate Santoña pact (24 August), which Franco did not honour. A pyramid-shaped memorial to the Italian dead still stands at the summit; the remains once kept there have since been moved.
look: A stone pyramid memorial beside the N-623 at the top of the pass, with wide mountain views.
plan: Pull in at the summit on the N-623 (Burgos–Santander). The road is often closed by snow in winter.
disputed: This is a Fascist-era monument; its future is debated under Spain's democratic memory legislation.

name: Oviedo siege – memorial to the defenders
text: On 19 July 1936 Colonel Antonio Aranda, who had persuaded Republican leaders he was loyal, declared for the rising and held Oviedo with soldiers, Civil Guards and Falangist volunteers. The city was surrounded by Asturian miners' militias. It survived months of siege, shelling and street fighting, including around the Plaza de la Constitución and the cathedral, until a Nationalist column from Galicia opened a narrow corridor on 16–17 October 1936. The Republican offensive of February 1937, supported by T-26 tanks, failed. The old centre was heavily damaged. A memorial to the city's killed defenders is kept at the town hall.
look: The town hall on Plaza de la Constitución, facing San Isidoro church, in an old quarter that was largely rebuilt after siege damage.
plan: Central Oviedo, on foot. Access to the memorial inside the town hall may be limited to opening hours.
disputed: Casualties: about 2,500 among the defenders and at least 5,000 among the attacking militias (Wikipedia); civilian deaths are unclear. Whether the memorial is still displayed has not been verified.

name: El Salvador cemetery mass grave, Oviedo
text: After Asturias fell in October 1937, Francoist courts-martial and extrajudicial killings claimed many lives. About 1,000 executions took place in Oviedo alone, and killings continued into the 1950s. Many of those shot against the walls of the municipal cemetery of El Salvador, at San Esteban de las Cruces, were buried in a common grave there. The names of 1,316 identified victims are now engraved on walls around the grave, making it one of the largest memorials of its kind in northern Spain. Earlier, in the Republican zone, rightists and clergy had also been killed in Asturias in 1934 and 1936.
look: Memorial walls engraved with the names of identified victims around the mass-grave area inside the cemetery.
plan: Open during cemetery hours; please be respectful. It is south of the city centre in San Esteban de las Cruces.
disputed: The overall death toll of post-war repression in Asturias is still being researched; 1,316 is the number of identified names on the memorial.

name: Monte Sollube battlefield
text: Sollube (686 m) commands the coast road between Bermeo and Bilbao. In May 1937 it was attacked by the mixed Italian-Spanish Flechas Negras brigade under Sandro Piazzoni and the IV Navarrese Brigade, supported by the Condor Legion. Basque, Asturian and Cantabrian battalions defended it, including UGT, ANV and Kirikiño units. The mountain fell around 8 May, and fighting on its slopes continued for several days. Roughly 1,000 men were killed on both sides. Losing Sollube opened the coastal approach to Bilbao's Iron Belt and was seen at the time as the beginning of the end for the city's defence.
look: An open mountain with wide views to Bermeo and the Urdaibai estuary; any remains of positions are informal and unsigned.
plan: The BI-631 Bilbao–Bermeo road crosses the Sollube pass; short walks to the summit start from the pass.
disputed: Casualty figures (about 400 Nationalist and 600 Republican dead) come from a single summary source.

name: Oviedo front – Cerdeño bunker
text: Once the Galician relief column had reached Oviedo in October 1936, the Nationalist defenders ringed the city with concrete positions facing the Republican lines on Monte Naranco and in the surrounding villages. Archaeologists have mapped many trenches and bunkers around Oviedo. They remained on a front line until Asturias fell in October 1937. The concrete bunker at Cerdeño, on the northern edge of the city below the Naranco, is one of the surviving Nationalist works. Just above rise the slopes of Monte Naranco, fought over repeatedly during the siege and the February 1937 offensive.
look: A concrete Nationalist bunker on the northern outskirts of Oviedo.
plan: On the edge of the village of Cerdeño, north of the city centre. Access may be over farmland, so ask before crossing fields.

name: Simancas barracks siege memorial, Gijón
text: When the coup failed in Gijón, Colonel Antonio Pinilla and about 600 soldiers of the Simancas mountain infantry regiment shut themselves into the Simancas barracks, a former Jesuit college. Asturian militias besieged them with dynamite, artillery and aircraft, while the Nationalist cruiser Almirante Cervera fired from offshore but could not relieve them. When the building was stormed in mid-August, Pinilla radioed the cruiser to fire on his own position. Almost the entire garrison died. The Franco regime made the siege a heroic legend, and a memorial to the regiment stands near the site.
look: A memorial to the Simancas regiment on Avenida Hermanos Felgueroso; the barracks building itself was later rebuilt.
plan: In the El Coto/La Arena area of Gijón, easy to reach on foot or by bus from the centre.
disputed: This is a Francoist commemorative monument; its current condition and status under democratic memory law have not been checked. Its exact position relative to the former barracks is uncertain.

name: Ceares cemetery mass grave, Gijón
text: After Gijón fell on 21 October 1937, thousands of Republicans were imprisoned and many were tried by courts-martial and shot. Victims executed at the wall of the Ceares municipal cemetery were buried in a common grave there. It is recorded as holding 1,293 victims of the war and the years that followed. It is now a place of annual remembrance for families and memory associations. The fall of Gijón ended the war in the North. Some Republican soldiers escaped to the mountains, and guerrilla resistance in Asturias went on for years.
look: A memorial area at the site of the common grave inside the municipal cemetery.
plan: Open during cemetery hours; please be quiet and respectful. It is south of the city centre in the Ceares district.

name: Astra factory air-raid shelter, Gernika
text: Gernika's arms industry, which made the famous Astra pistols, was one of the few potentially military targets in the town. In September 1936 the Talleres de Gernika factory built two concrete shelters for its workers. They were disguised under false roofs, and the bombers did not recognise them as shelters on 26 April 1937. The factory buildings on the edge of town largely survived the raid, a fact often cited in the debate over what the attack was really aiming at. The former Astra site is now a cultural centre.
look: A concrete shelter in the former Astra factory area on Ibarra Kalea.
plan: A 10-minute walk from the Peace Museum. Check with the tourist office about access to the interior.

name: Iron Belt Interpretation Centre, Berango
text: The Iron Belt's western end ran through the Uribe district north of Bilbao to the coast at Barrika and Sopela. Remains of bunkers, trenches and gun emplacements survive in Barrika, Berango, Sopela, Urduliz, Gatika, Loiu, Mungia and Zamudio, marked by information panels. The small interpretation centre in Berango has graphic panels and a display of objects and documents on how the line was built and why it failed in June 1937. It makes a good starting point for walks to the coastal and inland remains.
look: An exhibition of panels, objects and documents, plus signposted remains of the line in the surrounding municipalities.
plan: Check opening times with Uribe tourism before visiting. Walks to the coastal bunkers around Sopela and Berango take 1–2 h.
disputed: The coordinates are for Berango town centre; the centre's exact address has not been verified.
